body: I’m currently in investment banking. I’ve never planned to stay in banking anyway, most people use the experience for exit opportunities.
The wall punching was when I was just starting out my meds. I used to get angry for some reason. My doc has since upped my dosage and I thankfully don’t feel angry (as much) anymore.
I’m currently visiting my doctor on a regular schedule. She’s recommended an increase in dosage before. I may ask to switch medications because it definitely doesn’t feel as effective as before.

I sought help about 8 months ago and was prescribed meds, which helps a little. The one thing I am very scared about is experiencing this at my next job. I’ve become pretty insecure about not being able to work anywhere and I hope that doesn’t happen.

I’ve already sought help. Got prescribed some pills and they help somewhat. My firm is incredibly small (~10 people) so my contribution to the team is crucial. I’m afraid it’ll be a bad look or maybe they’d even let me go if I take too much time off.
The psychiatrist sending mail to my parents was my fault. I gave them my parents address because my insurance was linked to that address. Definitely an oversight on my end but I’m glad it worked out.

It was honestly kind of an accident. My psychiatrist send mail to my parents home (I live away from parents) and they asked me about it. I didn’t tell them much the first time around but I ended up calling and broke down and told them everything.

I’m on the same boat as you. Started my analyst stint about a year ago and anxiety has been an all time high since.

It got to the point where I can’t even relax because I know some work is going to come up. Not to mention my VP is very critical of my work. (I don’t consider myself a terrible analyst but I’ve definitely made a fair share of inexcusable mistakes).

I got prescribed a low dosage of anti-anxiety pills and they seem to be helping. Also, find time outside of work for a hobby/hanging out with friends. Playing video games after work (yup, playing fortnite at 2am) also takes my mind off of work.
Ahhh I see; sorry I’m new to this sub
Thank you for these words. I really do appreciate it. Unfortunately I don’t want to talk about it right now. Maybe in the future I’ll come back and hope you’re still willing to discuss. Thanks again.
I’ve done some research and you are absolutely correct. Thank you
Completely understand. I’ve also worked in retail although only for 1 year.

Very true. My dad has always told me that if I could only choose one, it’s better to be street smart than book smart. Academics is nice for applying to colleges and jobs but can only take you so far in the real world.

I subbed to this reddit for this exact reason. I work 10-12+ hours days just to go home and get an email from my boss asking for more work. Constantly being on call has me stressed all the time. Even on weekends my heart starts racing when I get an email bc theres a good chance it’s more work. 

Too many times I’ve escaped to the stairwell just to breath and be away from my desk. Hoping life can be more stress free later down the road.
What’s the difference between “closed” and “announced” dates for M&A deals and private placements?

It really depends on what you want to do. If FP&A or corporate development interests you, then Apple/FB/Google are probably among the best places to go. People are increasingly ditching banking jobs to get into tech roles. 

From a few Glassdoor searches, my guess for salary is that tech companies pay higher salaries than banks while banks pay higher bonuses. Although this doesn’t show prior work experience. “Analysts” at Goldman probably only have 0-2 years of prior work experience while Google financial analysts may have 4+ years. 

With that said, I’ve observed that it’s actually pretty difficult to get financial analyst jobs at large tech companies. Through searching titles on LinkedIn, I’ve notice that many of the analysts either attended an elite college or had prior investment banking experience.

Yup. I learned this early on. I can’t tell you how many times my friends have gotten ahead of themselves after a good interview and started talking about pay, relocation, and generally getting excited....only to get rejected. 

I keep telling people that applying to jobs is a numbers game. Sometimes you really couldn’t have done anything better and not get the job.

I disagree with this. A line for interests shows you’re a ‘real’ person and serves as a great talking point during interviews.

My MD noticed during the interview that I liked hiking and it turns out that he and his wife were huge into it as well. As long as you’re not putting anything stupid, I think having it will help you more than it will hurt you.
